speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) in the last five years, what have been the commonly reported forms of workplace discrimination; (b) whether there has been an increasing trend of discriminatory practices; and (c) how will the proposed Workplace Fairness Legislation address these issues.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what is the expected impact of the proposed Workplace Fairness Legislation on employer-employee relationships; (b) how does the Government intend to mitigate any negative impact, such as more litigious workplaces; and (c) how does the Government intend to mitigate the challenges that small firms may face, such as lack of human resource capabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Manpower besides Government legislation and guidelines on workplace fairness, what are the efforts needed to address the mindsets, attitudes and perceptions of individuals, to root out discrimination and build fairer workplaces.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: asked the Minister for Manpower how will the Government mitigate any negative impact of the proposed Workplace Fairness Legislation, such as a more litigious workplace culture.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether he can provide an update on the progress of the proposed Workplace Fairness Legislation; (b) when will the proposed legislation be implemented; (c) what are the possible negative impact of the proposed legislation; and (d) how will the Ministry manage any negative impact of the legislation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether there has been competing definitions of workplace discrimination between employers and employees raised during investigations conducted by the Ministry; and (b) how does the Ministry communicate what constitutes workplace discrimination to both employees and employers to help employees assess if they have a case and that employers are clear about their obligations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: asked the Minister for Manpower regarding the acts of discrimination that will be made clear in the proposed Workplace Fairness Legislation (a) how will the Ministry educate and make it clear to the public on unacceptable acts of discrimination; and (b) how will the Ministry assist employers, especially the smaller firms with limited human resource practitioners, understand more about discriminatory practices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If the questions have been addressed, it may not be necessary for them to proceed with the questions for future Sittings.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I wish to thank my Parliamentary colleagues for their interest in this important issue.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The proposed legislation is a significant step forward in enhancing protection for workers from workplace discrimination, as well as strengthening fair employment practices and outcomes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It builds on progressive efforts by the tripartite partners over the years to enhance workplace fairness through a range of education and enforcement efforts and will send a strong signal against workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is increasingly important in view of our ageing population and our marriage and parenthood efforts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It must also assure locals that they are fairly considered for job opportunities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Employers will benefit from a more productive and engaged workforce, be better able to attract and retain talent and can continue to access a complementary foreign workforce, contributing to stronger business outcomes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this way, the legislation will benefit workers, employers and society-at-large.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This was, indeed, the experience in the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In a study trip led by myself and our tripartite partners, we learned that the UK's Equality Act has had a positive impact on the workplace, and workers look to join organisations that operate fairly and treat all workers with respect.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is clearly in the interest of both employees and employers to create more trusting and harmonious workplaces by taking a strong stand against discrimination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Thus, strengthening our framework for workplace fairness through legislation is the right thing to do, but it should be done with an eye on maintaining a workplace culture that is harmonious and not litigious.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The steps have to be precise and clear, leaving little scope for subjective interpretation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This has always been one of the key objectives of the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness as we formulated our recommendations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is why we have tried to scope the recommendations more tightly and to the common and familiar forms of discrimination in the first instance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We believe it is better to take a measured first step, let our stakeholders adjust to the new rules before reviewing if more needs to be done.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The most common types of discrimination complaints received were on nationality, age, sex, race and language.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Committee has proposed that legislation provide protection against the common and familiar forms of workplace discrimination, including the characteristics I have just mentioned.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The legislation will work in tandem with the existing Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP) to cover all forms of workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I am heartened that Miss Rachel Ong, Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Edward Chia, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Miss Cheng Li Hui share the Committee's concern over the potential impact of legislation on workplace culture.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Indeed, workplace harmony is an invaluable hallmark of Singapore's employment landscape and needs to be protected, too.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, the Committee's recommendations focus on resolving disputes at the source as much as possible and emphasising mediation rather than litigation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To this end, the Committee recommends requiring employers to put in place grievance handling channels and processes at their workplace to facilitate amicable dispute resolution within the firm.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If that fails, mediation at the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) will be the next step, with a focus on educating employers on fair employment practices and mending the relationship between the employer and employee where possible.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Adjudication at the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT) is the last resort.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government will work closely with partners, including TAFEP and the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (ASME), to support small firms in their journey to ramp up capabilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: More details on this will be shared later.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I want to encourage smaller firms to work with the partners as early as possible to strengthen their human resource (HR) practices and capabilities, as well as nurture a fair and harmonious workplace culture.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As mentioned earlier, this will contribute to stronger business outcomes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Although exempted from the legislation at the start, small firms will continue to be subject to TGFEP, which prohibits all forms of workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Anyone who has faced any form of workplace discrimination can approach TAFEP for advice and assistance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Where there is a breach of TGFEP, TAFEP will report the case to MOM for enforcement action.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We agree with Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Sharael Taha that a coordinated and sustained effort by employers, employees, unions and the Government is required to educate all stakeholders and shape mindsets and attitudes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman also rightly points out that complaints of workplace discrimination may be borne out of different understandings of what constitutes discrimination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Today, TAFEP works closely with employer groups, HR partners and community groups to increase awareness of fair employment practices among employers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: TAFEP also offers workshops and training tools to help employers implement fair employment practices in their organisations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With the impending legislation, the tripartite partners will provide case illustrations of what may constitute discrimination and what may not, and regularly review and refresh these illustrations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The tripartite partners will also continue working closely to educate employers and workers to help advance fair and progressive employment practices in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It requires knowledge, understanding and ownership by employers, and support from employees.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Workplace Fairness Legislation will significantly strengthen our stand against discrimination, while maintaining a workplace culture that is harmonious and not litigious.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With regard to discrimination at breastfeeding mothers' phase, I thank the Senior Minister of State for sharing that the Committee is reviewing this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could I ask whether the Committee is engaging non-governmental organisations, like the Breastfeeding Mothers Support Group Singapore, to get their feedback and to consult them on this process?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, I do understand some forms of discriminations are not going to be covered under the proposed legislation and would be just covered under the Tripartite guidelines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could I ask the Senior Minister of State whether we can strengthen the penalties under the Tripartite guidelines?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because, again, as I raised many times in this House, it would not make sense if you discriminate against the women and the penalty is that you cannot hire foreigners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can strengthen those penalties to again send a very strong deterrent message.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will get the Committee to look at this and engage as widely as we can.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Whether the specific issue of breastfeeding ought to be one of the sub-characteristics, for example, within the sex category, that is something that the Committee will deliberate on.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We need to look at how we can also educate employers to ensure there is a more conducive workplace that will cater to all the diverse needs of their workers as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And when the legislation is tabled for discussion in Parliament, it will be clearer what levels of penalties may be effected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I just want to weigh in with what the Member Mr Louis Ng brought up about TGFEP and those characteristics that are not covered within the main piece of the legislation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I thought more teeth and more enforcement measures would help, particularly the investigative powers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My supplementary question would be, in this upcoming piece of Workplace Fairness Legislation, it is very important to take cognisance of the fact that we are going to help employees or workers in general.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are usually in a weaker bargaining position and usually do not have deep pockets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, I hope to see in this upcoming piece of legislation some form of tilting of the burden of proof towards them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Traditionally, you want to establish a prima facie case, you want reasonable doubt, but in different parts of the world, in certain jurisdictions, the burden is a bit lower, especially when employees and workers file complaints.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: So, I hope this can be taken cognisance of.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And we will take this into account when drafting the legislation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I must say that emphasis is also on ensuring that companies have in place a proper grievance handling process and that will include documentations about how to engage with employees when a complaint surfaces.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that can become one of the documented evidence when the adjudication needs to take place or where TADM needs to look at the dispute resolution between the employer and employee.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I believe that the process would be seen to be fair to both the employers and employees in this instance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of those complaints, can I confirm with the Senior Minister of State how many of them involve companies with a headcount of less than 25?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That would give us a sense of whether the five-year timeline is too long and whether it can be shortened or whether more work needs to be done to try and bring smaller firms up to speed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In our thinking and deliberation of initial exemptions for companies with less than 25 employees, it was really to give them more time to build up their capabilities and ability to deal with more of these workplace grievances, so that there is also time for stakeholders to engage smaller companies to up their capabilities to put into the grievance handling processes within the companies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is really more targeted towards building capacity.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Having said that, smaller companies today are already subjected to TGFEP, which also stipulate that all forms of discrimination are not to be tolerated at the workplace.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The only difference between the guidelines and the legislation is that the legislation allows us to have more finely calibrated penalties on the companies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The guidelines today allow MOM to take administrative measures against companies of any size which discriminate against a worker, by imposing, say, a blacklist for them to hire further foreign workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there is already some pain that we can inflict on companies which undertake discriminatory practices today under TGFEP.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But obviously, that is a very blunt approach and certain companies may find that such forbidding of hiring foreign workers over a case of infringement against one hiring of a Singaporean may become too overly excessive and impede the company's ability to function properly, thereby impacting the wider business operations that will impact a larger workforce within a company as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, in drafting the legislation, what we are trying to do is to have a graded approach of penalties that is more commensurate with the egregiousness of the company's offence in workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But companies with less than 25 in their workforce today will still have to follow TGFEP that forbids all forms of discrimination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I hope that clarifies that we are not letting smaller companies completely off the hook, but we are giving them more time to build their capabilities so that, through this process, we can build a more harmonious workplace and not a more litigious one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Just a quick supplementary question for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, I must say I am surprised but happy that the number of cases has gone down.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Having said that, we need to also pay attention to the number of unreported cases.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Personally, I am sure we have heard from many residents who come to us for these cases.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In firming up the framework that is coming up, I would like to suggest to the Senior Minister of State that we make it easy for people who feel aggrieved to report such cases.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, I hope that as the Ministry firms this up, let us make it easy for people to file such complaints.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there will be sufficient safeguards that we hope to put into the legislation to make sure that if any retaliatory action is taken by the employer against the employee, there will be penalties on the employers as well, just so that we can encourage those to step up to report any discrimination they face.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
